childhood and adult socio-environmental factors are associated with an increased likelihood of psychosis.
the effect of childhood adversity on risk of psychosis is mediated by adult disadvantage, and that childhood adversity and adult disadvantage combine synergistically to increase risk.
childhood and adult disadvantage are associated with an increased likelihood of psychosis.

the interplay between early and later adverse life experiences in the aetiology of psychosis.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
childhood and adult disadvantage combine to push some individuals into psychosis.
there is evidence that a combination of childhood and adult adversity may increase the risk of developing psychotic symptoms.
the effects of childhood and adult adversity are not additive, nor are they independent, but rather they interact to produce a greater effect than would be predicted by either factor alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is evidence that childhood and adult disadvantage combine in complex ways and that the effect of childhood disadvantage on psychosis may be mediated through subsequent adult disadvantage.
the effect of parental loss in childhood on psychosis risk may, in part, be mediated through subsequent educational attainment and adult social disadvantage.

there is a strong evidence that the effect on psychosis of separation from a parent in childhood is mediated through subsequent poor education, social disadvantage and, in a lesser degree, through low self-esteem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple pathways to psychosis and that it is important to identify the specific pathways for each individual.
the effects of childhood and adult socioenvironmental factors on risk of psychosis may be better understood by considering them together.
